context: marine + industrial · dry dock or ship lift, quays, giant cranes and fabrication halls

brief.intro: New to this project type? Building a shipyard combines heavy marine works with a large factory. On the water side there is a dry dock (a huge concrete basin with a gate that can be pumped dry) or a ship lift with transfer rails, plus quay walls where ships are fitted out afloat, all needing dredging. On the land side there are steel stockyards, cutting and panel lines, block-assembly halls, blasting and painting cells, outfitting workshops, and very heavy paved areas over which blocks weighing hundreds of tonnes are moved. Above everything stand the cranes — a goliath gantry crane spanning the dock and jib cranes along the quays. The dry dock is the longest and riskiest item (deep excavation below sea level, dewatering, a thick floor and the dock gate); the goliath crane is the longest-lead purchase.

must_get_right: Start the dry dock first: cofferdam, deep excavation, dewatering, floor and walls, gate and pump house form the longest chain, and ground conditions are its main risk.
Order the goliath crane and the dock gate early — both are bespoke, take over a year, and the crane's rails and foundations must be built to its exact loads.
Marine works (dredging, quay walls) depend on permits, marine plant and weather; sequence them so the cofferdam can be removed and the dock flooded when the gate is ready.

The halls follow the production flow of steel (stockyard → cutting → panels → blocks → paint → dock); build and commission them in that order so trial production can start before the dock is finished.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by facility (dock, quays, each hall, cranes, utilities) following the yard's production flow.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar; marine works depend on tide, sea state and season; dewatering runs continuously.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Permits → dredging and reclamation → cofferdam → dock excavation → floor and walls → gate sill → dock systems and gate → cofferdam removal → flooding. In parallel: quay walls; halls in production-flow order; crane rails → crane erection → load tests; utilities. The critical path runs through the dry dock, or the goliath crane.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Marine permits are granted on the assumed date; ground and groundwater are as investigated; the grid can supply the yard's demand.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule tracks the following as milestones because they drive the programme:

rows: Before block erection in the dock

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Work below sea level behind a cofferdam; heavy-lift erection of the goliath crane needs a wind-free window and clear ground; marine plant availability.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: ground conditions and seepage in the dock excavation, cofferdam stability, late crane or gate, settlement of reclaimed land under heavy paving, and marine weather. Contingency is held before dock flooding.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by facility and structure; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the marine, structural and crane-erection crews — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
